display_name: Fritz Haag Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Riesling Auslese, Mosel
raw_content:
{
  "hook": "The Sonnenuhr vineyard's steep slate slopes are so steep they face south to catch every ray of sun, yet the 2020 vintage delivered a surprising freshness that cuts through the wine's 160 g/L of residual sugar. This Auslese from the Juffer parcel sits above the famous Sonnenuhr sundial site, where the slate soil forces Riesling roots deep for mineral extraction.",
  "wine_summary": "Fritz Haag's Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Auslese represents the pinnacle of sweet Riesling from one of the Mosel's most iconic sites. The Juffer parcel sits directly above the Sonnenuhr vineyard, where the slate soil is so steep that vines must be trained on high wires to receive sunlight. The 2020 vintage produced wines with remarkable concentration and acidity balance, with ABV typically around 7.5% despite the high sugar levels. This wine matters because it demonstrates how slate-driven mineral intensity can coexist with honeyed richness, creating a tension that defines great Mosel Riesling.",
  "terroir_expression": "The blue slate soil of the Juffer parcel creates the wine's distinctive flinty, smoky character that persists through the sweetness. The Mosel's cool continental climate with late autumn fog concentrates sugars while preserving the grape's natural acidity, allowing Auslese-level ripeness without losing vibrancy. The southwest-facing slopes at Brauneberger Juffer achieve optimal sun exposure despite the region's northern latitude, while the slate's heat retention extends the growing season. This geological foundation translates directly to the glass: the wine's electric acidity and mineral backbone provide structure that prevents the 160+ g/L of residual sugar from becoming cloying.",
  "vinification_summary": "Fritz Haag practices traditional Mosel winemaking with spontaneous fermentation in large, neutral oak casks that allow the wine to develop without oak influence. The winery selects only botrytis-affected berries for Auslese, which concentrates sugars and creates the characteristic honeyed notes. The key technical concept is 'Spätlese' selection timing—Haag waits until grapes reach Auslese-level sugar concentration (typically 20-22° Oechsle) while maintaining acidity, then hand-harvestes in multiple passes. Fermentation is stopped naturally when alcohol reaches 7-8%, preserving the wine's balance between sugar and acidity.",
  "food_pairing": [
    "Nashville hot chicken: The wine's high acidity and residual sugar cut through the cayenne heat while the mineral backbone stands up to fried chicken skin and sweet pickles.",
    "Foie gras torchon with brioche: The honeyed richness mirrors the liver's buttery texture while the wine's acidity cleanses the palate between bites.",
    "Spicy Szechuan mapo tofu: The sugar tames the chili heat while the wine's citrus notes complement the fermented bean paste and scallions.",
    "Roasted pork belly with apple compote: The wine's stone fruit and honey notes echo the compote while acidity balances the fat.",
    "Blue cheese and honeycomb: The classic sweet-salty contrast works because the wine's mineral character cuts through the cheese's pungency while the sugar highlights the honey."
  ],
  "comparable_wines": [
    "Dr. Loosen Bernkasteler Lay Auslese — Similar slate-driven mineral character from a neighboring Mosel village, though slightly less concentrated due to different vineyard exposure.",
    "Egon Müller Scharzhofberger Auslese — The benchmark for Mosel Auslese from a different famous site, with comparable acidity-sugar balance but a more opulent style."
  ],
  "style_profile": "Off-dry white Riesling with electric acidity, medium body, and slate-driven mineral intensity",
  "cellar_recommendation": "This wine will develop beautifully for 20+ years, with the acidity preserving freshness as the honeyed notes deepen. Store at 55°F in a dark, humid cellar and drink from 2025 through 2045.",
  "value_assessment": "At $80-120 per bottle, this wine competes directly with Dr. Loosen Bernkasteler Lay Auslese ($70-90) and Egon Müller Scharzhofberger Auslese ($150-200). The price is justified by the site's reputation and the labor-intensive selection process for botrytis-affected berries, making it worth it for serious Riesling collectors.",
  "market_position": "Serious Riesling collectors and fine dining restaurants with adventurous wine programs drive demand for this wine. It appears on Michelin-starred restaurant lists and specialty wine shops with strong German wine selections, while casual drinkers rarely encounter it due to the $80+ price point and sweetness level.",
  "insider_take": "Most people dismiss sweet Riesling as unserious, but this Auslese's mineral backbone and acidity make it as structured as many dry wines. The real tradeoff is that the sugar intensity can overshadow food if you're not pairing it with something spicy or fatty to balance the sweetness.",

parsed.hook: The Sonnenuhr vineyard's steep slate slopes are so steep they face south to catch every ray of sun, yet the 2020 vintage delivered a surprising freshness that cuts through the wine's 160 g/L of residual sugar. This Auslese from the Juffer parcel sits above the famous Sonnenuhr sundial site, where the slate soil forces Riesling roots deep for mineral extraction.
parsed.wine_summary: Fritz Haag's Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr Auslese represents the pinnacle of sweet Riesling from one of the Mosel's most iconic sites. The Juffer parcel sits directly above the Sonnenuhr vineyard, where the slate soil is so steep that vines must be trained on high wires to receive sunlight. The 2020 vintage produced wines with remarkable concentration and acidity balance, with ABV typically around 7.5% despite the high sugar levels. This wine matters because it demonstrates how slate-driven mineral intensity can coexist with honeyed richness, creating a tension that defines great Mosel Riesling.
parsed.terroir_expression: The blue slate soil of the Juffer parcel creates the wine's distinctive flinty, smoky character that persists through the sweetness. The Mosel's cool continental climate with late autumn fog concentrates sugars while preserving the grape's natural acidity, allowing Auslese-level ripeness without losing vibrancy. The southwest-facing slopes at Brauneberger Juffer achieve optimal sun exposure despite the region's northern latitude, while the slate's heat retention extends the growing season. This geological foundation translates directly to the glass: the wine's electric acidity and mineral backbone provide structure that prevents the 160+ g/L of residual sugar from becoming cloying.
parsed.vinification_summary: Fritz Haag practices traditional Mosel winemaking with spontaneous fermentation in large, neutral oak casks that allow the wine to develop without oak influence. The winery selects only botrytis-affected berries for Auslese, which concentrates sugars and creates the characteristic honeyed notes. The key technical concept is 'Spätlese' selection timing—Haag waits until grapes reach Auslese-level sugar concentration (typically 20-22° Oechsle) while maintaining acidity, then hand-harvestes in multiple passes. Fermentation is stopped naturally when alcohol reaches 7-8%, preserving the wine's balance between sugar and acidity.

Roasted pork belly with apple compote: The wine's stone fruit and honey notes echo the compote while acidity balances the fat.
Blue cheese and honeycomb: The classic sweet-salty contrast works because the wine's mineral character cuts through the cheese's pungency while the sugar highlights the honey.

parsed.insider_take: Most people dismiss sweet Riesling as unserious, but this Auslese's mineral backbone and acidity make it as structured as many dry wines. The real tradeoff is that the sugar intensity can overshadow food if you're not pairing it with something spicy or fatty to balance the sweetness.
